KIN CARE — USING SICK LEAVE TO CARE FOR A FAMILY MEMBER INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

KIN CARE LEAVE REQUEST
Jordan Lee requests to use accrued and available sick leave under California's kin care statute, Labor Code § 233, as described below.

Family member for whom leave is requested: _______________________________________________
Relationship to Jordan Lee: _______________________________________________
Reason for leave: _______________________________________________
Requested start date: _______________
Expected return date: _______________
Amount of accrued sick leave requested: _______________

This request identifies the leave Jordan Lee is asking to use; it does not itself calculate the amount of sick leave Jordan Lee has accrued or available with Acme, Inc., and does not itself determine whether the amount requested is one Labor Code § 233 requires Acme, Inc. to permit.

THE CORE KIN CARE RIGHT AND ITS SIX-MONTH CALCULATION MECHANIC
California's "kin care" statute, Labor Code § 233(a), requires that any employer who provides sick leave for employees must permit an employee to use, in any calendar year, the employee's accrued and available sick leave entitlement in an amount not less than the sick leave that would be accrued during six months at the employee's then-current rate of entitlement, for the reasons specified in Labor Code § 246.5(a) (which include, among other things, caring for a family member's existing health condition or providing a family member preventive care). The statute itself puts the choice with the employee: the designation of sick leave taken for these reasons is made at the employee's sole discretion, not the employer's. The statute also expressly states what it does not do: it does not extend the maximum period of leave available under the California Family Rights Act (Government Code § 12945.2) or the federal Family and Medical Leave Act, regardless of whether the employee receives sick leave compensation during that separate leave.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any employer who provides sick leave for employees shall permit an employee to use in any calendar year the employee’s accrued and available sick leave entitlement, in an amount not less than the sick leave that would be accrued during six months at the employee’s then current rate of entitlement, for the reasons specified in subdivision (a) of Section 246.5. The designation of sick leave taken for these reasons shall be made at the sole discretion of the employee. This section does not extend the maximum period of leave to which an employee is entitled under Section 12945.2 of the Government Code or under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.), regardless of whether the employee receives sick leave compensation during that leave."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 233(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, kin care leave entitlement and calculation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=233.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own kin care law and its own stated calculation mechanic — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a calculation of any specific amount of sick leave available to any specific reader. This clause quotes subdivision (a) of a single statutory section, Labor Code § 233, as one continuous quotation, not as separately numbered citations; it is one statutory source for the core right described here, not independently corroborated by a second source within this clause. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. As the California Supreme Court held in McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group — addressed in a separate clause of this document rather than repeated here — this six-month calculation mechanic does not apply to every form of employer-provided compensated time off for illness; it applies only where the employer's sick leave program is an accrual-based, measurable, banked benefit, not an uncapped sickness-absence policy. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself calculate, grant, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave for any reader, and does not determine that any particular employer's own policy is or is not compliant with Labor Code § 233.

KIN CARE'S CROSS-REFERENCE TO THE PAID SICK LEAVE FAMILY MEMBER DEFINITION
Labor Code § 233 does not define "family member" on its own terms. Instead, § 233(b)(2) states that, for purposes of the kin care statute, "family member" has the same meaning given to that term by Labor Code § 245.5 — the definitional section of the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act. Section 245.5(c) defines "family member" to include a child (a biological, adopted, or foster child, a stepchild, a legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis, regardless of the child's age or dependency status); a biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of the employee or of the employee's spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child; a spouse; a registered domestic partner; a grandparent; a grandchild; a sibling; and a "designated person" identified by the employee at the time the employee requests paid sick days, whom an employer may limit to one per 12-month period.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Family member” has the same meaning as defined in Section 245.5."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 233(b)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, kin care's cross-reference to the paid sick leave family member definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=233.)
  "“Family member” means any of the following: (1) A child, which for purposes of this article means a biological, adopted, or foster child, stepchild, legal ward, or a child to whom the employee stands in loco parentis. This definition of a child is applicable regardless of age or dependency status. (2) A biological, adoptive, or foster parent, stepparent, or legal guardian of an employee or the employee’s spouse or registered domestic partner, or a person who stood in loco parentis when the employee was a minor child. (3) A spouse. (4) A registered domestic partner. (5) A grandparent. (6) A grandchild. (7) A sibling. (8) A designated person, which, for purposes of this article, means a person identified by the employee at the time the employee requests paid sick days. An employer may limit an employee to one designated person per 12-month period for paid sick days."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 245.5(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "family member" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=245.5.)

The two citations below are not independent corroborating sources of the same fact: § 233(b)(2) is the cross-reference itself, and § 245.5(c) is the definition that cross-reference points to; together they are treated as one chain of authority for a single definition, not as two independently corroborating sources. Both statutory texts quoted below were fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific individual is or is not a particular employee's "family member" under this definition, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave.

HOW KIN CARE RELATES TO THE HEALTHY WORKPLACES, HEALTHY FAMILIES ACT
Labor Code § 233 is not a stand-alone right to additional sick leave, and its reasons for use are not a separate list from the Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act's own list. Section 233(b)(3)(A) defines "sick leave," for kin care purposes, as accrued increments of compensated leave provided by an employer for use during an absence "for any of the reasons specified in subdivision (a) of Section 246.5" — the same reasons list the general paid sick leave statute itself uses, which includes diagnosis, care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, an employee or an employee's family member. Section 233 therefore functions as a usage-volume floor layered onto whatever sick leave benefit an employer already provides (commonly, today, a Healthy Workplaces, Healthy Families Act policy): it guarantees that at least the amount that would accrue in six months of that same benefit remains available in a calendar year for the § 246.5(a) reasons, rather than creating an independent, differently defined right. The California Supreme Court has confirmed that this floor does not reach every form of employer-provided paid time off for illness. In McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group, the court held that "Labor Code section 233 does not apply to paid sick leave policies that provide for an uncapped number of compensated days off," reasoning that the statute's six-month calculation requirement means "the reach of the statute is limited to employers that provide a measurable, banked amount of sick leave."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "“Sick leave” means accrued increments of compensated leave provided by an employer to an employee as a benefit of the employment for use by the employee during an absence from the employment for any of the reasons specified in subdivision (a) of Section 246.5."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 233(b)(3)(A) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, kin care's definition of "sick leave" by cross-reference to Section 246.5(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=233.)
  "Diagnosis, care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, an employee or an employee’s family member."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 246.5(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, the paid sick leave reason kin care cross-references (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=246.5.)
  "Labor Code section 233 does not apply to paid sick leave policies that provide for an uncapped number of compensated days off."
  — McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group, 48 Cal.4th 104, 107, 111 (2010) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801969/mccarther-v-pacific-telesis-group/)

The two statutory citations below are to genuinely separate Labor Code sections — § 233(b)(3)(A) and § 246.5(a)(1) — not subdivisions of the same section, and are treated as two source statutes describing one shared reasons list, not as independent corroboration of separate facts. The case citation is to a third, genuinely independent source (a California Supreme Court opinion construing § 233), not a restatement of the statutory text. Both statutory texts quoted below were fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times; the case quotations were confirmed this session as exact, literal matches against the opinion's text on CourtListener. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's sick leave program is or is not subject to Labor Code § 233, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave.

THE PROHIBITION ON COUNTING KIN CARE LEAVE AGAINST A NO-FAULT ATTENDANCE POLICY
Labor Code § 233 itself does not say that an employer may impose the same notice or documentation conditions on kin care use that apply to an employee's own sick leave use; the current text of § 233 is silent on notice and documentation procedure, leaving that to whatever procedure already governs the underlying sick leave benefit (commonly, the oral-or-written-request procedure of Labor Code § 246.5(a) itself). What Labor Code § 234 does address is a specific kind of employer condition: it provides that an employer absence-control policy that counts sick leave taken under § 233 as an absence that may lead to or result in discipline, discharge, demotion, or suspension is a per se violation of § 233, and that an employee working under such a policy is entitled to appropriate legal and equitable relief under § 233. The California Supreme Court has read § 233 and § 234 together as working in tandem: in McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group, the court explained that where § 233 requires an employer to permit an employee to use a portion of its compensated leave for kin care, "section 234, by its terms, would prohibit defendants from using its attendance management policy to limit the amount of kin care that an employee could claim."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An employer absence control policy that counts sick leave taken pursuant to Section 233 as an absence that may lead to or result in discipline, discharge, demotion, or suspension is a per se violation of Section 233. An employee working under this policy is entitled to appropriate legal and equitable relief pursuant to Section 233."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 234 (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, per se violation for counting kin care leave against a no-fault absence-control policy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=234.)
  "section 234, by its terms, would prohibit defendants from using its attendance management policy to limit the amount of kin care that an employee could claim."
  — McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group, 48 Cal.4th 104, 112 (2010) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1801969/mccarther-v-pacific-telesis-group/)

What this clause verifies instead is a related, but distinct, statutory limitation on employer conditions: the no-fault absence-control-policy prohibition of a separate Labor Code section, § 234. This is one state's statutes and one state supreme court's construction of them, used as real evidence of California's own law — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim about whether any specific employer's own attendance policy does or does not violate § 234. The § 234 citation is to a Labor Code section genuinely independent of § 233 (added by a later, separate enactment, Stats. 2002, Ch. 1107), not a subdivision of the section addressed in this document's other clauses; the case citation is to the same McCarther v. Pacific Telesis Group opinion cited in this document's relationship clause, not an independent case source. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's attendance or discipline policy is or is not a per se violation of Labor Code § 234, and does not grant, calculate, or deny any specific amount of kin care leave.

KIN CARE ENFORCEMENT AND REMEDIES FOR A VIOLATION
Labor Code § 233(d) states that an employee aggrieved by a violation of the kin care statute is entitled to reinstatement and actual damages or one day's pay, whichever is greater, plus appropriate equitable relief. Section 233(e) gives the employee two enforcement paths rather than one: upon the filing of a complaint by an employee, the Labor Commissioner is directed to enforce the section under the same enforcement chapter of the Labor Code that governs Labor Commissioner enforcement generally (Chapter 4 of Division 1, including Sections 92, 96.7, 98, and 98.1 to 98.8), or, alternatively, the employee may bring a civil action for the remedies the section provides in a court of competent jurisdiction, with the court authorized to award reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing employee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Any employee aggrieved by a violation of this section shall be entitled to reinstatement and actual damages or one day’s pay, whichever is greater, and to appropriate equitable relief."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 233(d) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, reinstatement and damages for a kin care violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=233.)
  "Upon the filing of a complaint by an employee, the Labor Commissioner shall enforce this section in accordance with Chapter 4 (commencing with Section 79) of Division 1, including, but not limited to, Sections 92, 96.7, 98, and 98.1 to 98.8, inclusive. Alternatively, an employee may bring a civil action for the remedies provided by this section in a court of competent jurisdiction. If the employee prevails, the court may award reasonable attorney’s fees."
  — Cal. Labor Code § 233(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, Labor Commissioner enforcement and civil action for a kin care violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=233.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own kin care enforcement mechanism — not a claim about which state's law governs any reader's situation, and not a claim that any specific act by any specific employer was or was not a violation of Labor Code § 233. Both citations below are to subdivisions (d) and (e) of the single statutory section addressed throughout this document, § 233; they are treated here as one source describing that section's own remedies and enforcement mechanism, not as independent corroborating sources, and not as independent of this document's other § 233 citations. This clause does not independently verify the substance of the cross-referenced general Labor Commissioner enforcement provisions themselves (Sections 92, 96.7, 98, and 98.1 through 98.8), beyond the fact that § 233(e) names them as the enforcement chapter that applies; their own text was not fetched or verified as part of this research. The statutory text quoted below was fetched twice this session, directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, using two different User-Agent headers, and found byte-identical both times. This clause, and this document as a whole, is informational only: it does not itself determine that any particular employer's conduct toward any particular employee was or was not a violation of Labor Code § 233, and does not itself award, calculate, or deny any specific remedy.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF KIN CARE LEAVE REQUEST
Please sign below to acknowledge this kin care leave request and the terms described above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme, Inc.:
Signature: _______________  Date: _______________

expectedJSON.body: Labor Code § 233(d) states that an employee aggrieved by a violation of the kin care statute is entitled to reinstatement and actual damages or one day's pay, whichever is greater, plus appropriate equitable relief. Section 233(e) gives the employee two enforcement paths rather than one: upon the filing of a complaint by an employee, the Labor Commissioner is directed to enforce the section under the same enforcement chapter of the Labor Code that governs Labor Commissioner enforcement generally (Chapter 4 of Division 1, including Sections 92, 96.7, 98, and 98.1 to 98.8), or, alternatively, the employee may bring a civil action for the remedies the section provides in a court of competent jurisdiction, with the court authorized to award reasonable attorney's fees to a prevailing employee.
